question: Which minerals led the price declines in 2026Q3, and by how much did they fall?
expected_answer: Cobalt fell 25 percent (q/q) and lithium 13 percent.

gold.evidence_quote: led by cobalt, which fell by 25 percent (q/q), and lithium, which declined by 13 percent

hits.text:
Other critical minerals
Prices of other critical minerals generally weakened in 2026Q3, led by cobalt, which fell by 25 percent (q/q), and lithium, which declined by 13 percent (figure 20.A). The decline in lithium prices reflected the restart of previously curtailed mines in Australia, the resumption of concentrate exports from Zimbabwe, and softer EV sales momentum in China, although strong demand from energy storage and robust EV demand in several other regions provided support. Cobalt prices fell sharply, partly reversing earlier gains, but remained elevated as export quotas in the Democratic Republic of Congo continued to constrain global supply. Rare earth prices were broadly stable, with ongoing Chinese export controls and licensing requirements curbing supply in some markets outside China.

Base metals and iron ore
Recent developments and outlook
Average base metal prices edged lower in 2026Q3 and declined further in October, although aluminum, copper, tin, and zinc reached all-time highs. In contrast, iron ore prices declined in the quarter, recently averaging about 40 percent below their 2011 peak level (figure 19.A). Tightness in several base metal markets has partly reflected supply constraints, including disruptions at major mines and smelters, and official production limits in China. Rapidly growing investment in power grids, electric vehicle (EV) production, renewable energy, electronics, and data centers continued to support demand for aluminum, copper, and tin. Meanwhile, the ongoing slump in construction and steel activity—particularly in China—weighed on iron ore prices.

Critical mineral prices generally weakened in 2026Q3, with cobalt and lithium falling while rare earth prices were broadly stable. However, supply restrictions continued to support prices in some markets. New trade-
policy interventions have remained common, with restrictive measures far outnumbering liberalizing actions in recent years. Export restrictions and strategic stockpiling could lift international prices in the near term, while efforts to expand mining, processing, and recycling capacity may gradually improve supply resilience. Yet with demand projected to rise sharply and new projects facing long lead times, critical mineral markets are expected to remain highly sensitive to policy changes and disruptions for some time.

question: On what share of trading days does silver rank among the three biggest net transmitters of volatility?

gold.evidence_quote: silver ranks among the three largest net-transmitting commodities on almost 60 percent of trading days
and silver in almost 60 percent

hits.text:
• Price volatility transmission is highly uneven across commodity groups. Industrial metals and food are the principal net transmitters, as they transmit much more volatility than they receive. Livestock and soft commodities are at the other end of the spectrum, as they receive considerably more volatility than they transmit. Energy and precious metals occupy an intermediate position as they transmit and receive broadly similar amounts of volatility.
• Transmission is concentrated in a small number of individual commodity markets. Copper, maize, oil, and silver stand out as important bridges across commodity groups. Their roles differ in persistence: silver ranks among the three largest net-transmitting commodities on almost 60 percent of trading days, maize in about half, copper in just over 40 percent, and oil the least frequently, reflecting its more episode-specific importance.

Copper, maize, oil, and silver are therefore pivotal commodities bridging the commodity network for distinct reasons, but the persistence of their influence differs. Oil ranks among the three largest net transmitters in only 10 percent of trading days, reflecting its more episode-specific importance. Copper does so in just over 40 percent of trading days, maize in about half, and silver in almost 60 percent. Silver is structurally positioned in two parts of the system, combining financial and safe-haven demand with extensive industrial use, and therefore links precious metals to the industrial block irrespective of the prevailing state of the cycle (Mensi et al. 2023).

Transmitters and receivers
Commodity groups can be similarly connected to the broader system while playing very different roles within it. Directional connectedness separates volatility transmitted to other groups from volatility received from them. The full-sample results show a clear hierarchy: industrial metals and food transmit more volatility than they receive; livestock and soft commodities receive more than they transmit; and energy and precious metals are broadly balanced between the two roles (figure SF .1.D).
Net connectedness—the difference between transmitted and received connectedness—provides the clearest summary of this hierarchy. Industrial metals and food have net connectedness indexes of about 11 and 7, respectively, and their transmitted connectedness is roughly 64 to 75 percent greater than their received connectedness. Livestock and soft commodities have net indexes of approximately −4 and −8 and transmit only about half as much volatility as they receive.
